q: How does React's Fiber architecture work internally? What problem does it solve over the old stack reconciler?
a:
The old stack reconciler (React ≤15) processed the entire component tree synchronously in one uninterruptible call stack. A large update could block the main thread for tens of milliseconds, dropping frames and making the UI feel janky.

Fiber (React 16+) reimplemented reconciliation as a linked list of "fiber nodes" — one per component instance. Each fiber stores the component type, its props/state, pointers to parent/child/sibling fibers, and a work tag (what needs to happen). This structure lets React:

  • Split rendering work into small units that can be paused between browser frames
  • Assign different priorities to different updates (a keypress is more urgent than a background data fetch)
  • Abandon and restart work if a higher-priority update arrives
  • Reuse already-completed work when possible

The process has two phases: render/reconcile phase (interruptible — can be paused, resumed, or thrown away; runs in memory) and commit phase (synchronous and non-interruptible — applies all DOM mutations at once). This split is why effects run after the browser has painted.

In interviews: emphasize the render/commit split and why the render phase being interruptible requires render functions (including function component bodies and hooks like useMemo) to be pure and side-effect-free — they may run more than once for a single committed render.
source: sudheerj/reactjs-interview-questions, React docs (react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state), common senior interview pattern

q: What is the rules-of-hooks constraint and why does React enforce it?
a:
React's two rules of hooks are: (1) only call hooks at the top level — never inside loops, conditionals, or nested functions; (2) only call hooks from React function components or custom hooks — not from regular JS functions.

The reason is purely about order. React has no names for your hooks — it tracks them by their call order on each render. Internally, each hook call maps to a slot in a linked list attached to the fiber. If you conditionally call a hook, the list position shifts between renders, and React reads the wrong state value for the wrong hook.

// BAD — conditional hook
if (condition) {
  const [val, setVal] = useState(0) // slot 2 sometimes, slot 1 other times
}

// OK — condition inside the hook
const [val, setVal] = useState(0)
const active = condition ? val : defaultValue

The eslint-plugin-react-hooks (exhaustive-deps + rules-of-hooks) catches violations statically. This is frequently asked at senior level because it reveals whether the candidate understands hooks as ordered array slots rather than magic.
source: React docs (react.dev/reference/rules/rules-of-hooks), sudheerj/reactjs-interview-questions Q21, GreatFrontEnd React quiz

q: Explain the useLayoutEffect hook. When should you use it instead of useEffect?
a:
useEffect runs asynchronously after the browser has painted. useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM mutations but before the browser paints.

The timing difference matters for:

  • Reading DOM layout (dimensions, scroll position, bounding rects) and using those values to make further DOM mutations. If done in useEffect, the user sees a flash of the wrong layout before the correction paints.
  • Imperative DOM positioning (tooltips, popovers that need to measure their anchor before appearing)
  • Keeping a ref always up-to-date before the next paint (e.g., panRef and applyTransform() in SVG pan/zoom)
useLayoutEffect(() => {
  const { width } = ref.current.getBoundingClientRect()
  setWidth(width) // safe — no flash
})

Important caveats: useLayoutEffect blocks painting, so expensive work here degrades perceived performance. On the server (SSR) it does not run at all — React 18 emits a warning; use useEffect or suppress with suppressHydrationWarning. Prefer useEffect by default; reach for useLayoutEffect only when you can observe a visual flicker with useEffect.
source: React docs (react.dev/reference/react/useLayoutEffect), GreatFrontEnd, common senior interview

q: What is automatic batching in React 18 and how does it differ from React 17?
a:
Batching means React groups multiple setState calls into a single re-render to avoid unnecessary work.

In React 17 and earlier, batching only happened inside React event handlers (onClick, onChange, etc.). setState calls inside setTimeout, Promise.then, native event listeners, or async functions each triggered their own separate re-render:

// React 17 — 2 separate renders inside setTimeout
setTimeout(() => {
  setCount(c => c + 1)  // render 1
  setFlag(f => !f)      // render 2
}, 1000)

In React 18 with createRoot, batching is automatic in all contexts — event handlers, timeouts, promises, native events. Both setStates above become one render.

Opting out: if you genuinely need separate renders (rare), use ReactDOM.flushSync:

import { flushSync } from 'react-dom'
flushSync(() => setCount(c => c + 1))  // forces immediate render
flushSync(() => setFlag(f => !f))      // second render

Interview tip: mention that automatic batching is one reason migrating to createRoot (the React 18 entry point) can improve perceived performance with zero code changes in components.

q: How does React's key prop work during reconciliation? What are the consequences of using array index as key?
a:
The key prop is React's identity signal for elements in a list. During reconciliation, React pairs elements from the previous tree with elements from the new tree by key. If keys match, React updates (reuses) the existing DOM node and component instance. If a key disappears or a new one appears, React destroys or creates accordingly.

Using index as key works correctly only when:

  • The list is static (never reordered, filtered, or prepended)
  • List items have no state or uncontrolled inputs

Index as key breaks in these scenarios:

  • Reordering: item B moves from index 1 to index 0. React sees key=0 unchanged and tries to update item A's DOM node with item B's data — component state (scroll position, form input, animation) stays on the wrong item.
  • Prepending: inserting at the beginning shifts all indices. React remounts every item unnecessarily.
  • Deletion from middle: same key-shift problem.
// Correct — stable, unique identity
{items.map(item => <Row key={item.id} data={item} />)}

Intentional remounting with key: setting a key on a non-list component forces React to destroy and recreate it when the key changes — a clean way to reset internal state (e.g., resetting a form when the user ID changes): <ProfileForm key={userId} />.

q: What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled components? When would you choose each?
a:
A controlled component has its form value driven by React state. Every keystroke calls onChange, which calls setState, which re-renders with the new value. React is the single source of truth.

const [val, setVal] = useState('')
<input value={val} onChange={e => setVal(e.target.value)} />

An uncontrolled component stores its value in the DOM. You read it imperatively via a ref when needed (on submit, on blur). The DOM is the source of truth.

const ref = useRef()
<input defaultValue="" ref={ref} />
// on submit: ref.current.value

Choose controlled when:

  • You need to validate or transform input on every keystroke
  • You need to programmatically set the value (e.g., fill from autocomplete)
  • Multiple fields depend on each other's values
  • You need instant UI feedback (character count, live preview)

Choose uncontrolled when:

  • Simple one-time-read forms (login, search) where per-keystroke re-renders add no value
  • Integrating with non-React code or third-party DOM libraries
  • Performance-critical forms with many fields (large forms with controlled state can be slow without memoization)

Libraries like React Hook Form take the uncontrolled approach internally (using refs) and expose a controlled-like API — combining best-of-both-worlds performance and developer experience.
source: sudheerj/reactjs-interview-questions Q18, React docs, GreatFrontEnd React

q: Explain React's Suspense mechanism. How does it work with data fetching and what changed in React 18?
a:
Suspense lets a component "suspend" rendering while it waits for something (data, lazy-loaded code) and show a fallback in the meantime — without the component knowing it's suspended.

How it works: A Suspense-aware data source (React.lazy, a framework like Next.js/Remix, or a library like SWR/React Query with Suspense mode) throws a Promise during render. React catches it, climbs the tree to find the nearest <Suspense> boundary, renders the fallback, and retries the subtree when the promise resolves.

const LazyChart = React.lazy(() => import('./Chart'))

<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
  <LazyChart />
</Suspense>

React 18 additions:

  • Suspense on the server: streaming HTML. The server sends the shell immediately and streams suspended subtrees as they resolve, hydrating them incrementally — eliminating the "all-or-nothing" SSR waterfall.
  • Selective hydration: React prioritizes hydrating the part the user is interacting with first.
  • SuspenseList (experimental): coordinates reveal order of multiple Suspense boundaries.

Key interview point: do not fetch inside useEffect in Suspense-enabled architectures — the component renders before the effect runs, producing a loading flash (request waterfall). Fetch in the render path (via a Suspense-compatible library) or in a Server Component.
source: React docs (react.dev/reference/react/Suspense), React 18 release blog, sudheerj advanced section

q: How do you correctly type React component props with TypeScript? Explain the difference between FC<Props> and defining props inline. What is the children prop typing pattern?
a:
There are two main approaches to typing function component props:

1. Explicit props interface (preferred):

interface ButtonProps {
  label: string
  onClick: () => void
  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary'
}

function Button({ label, onClick, variant = 'primary' }: ButtonProps) {
  return <button onClick={onClick}>{label}</button>
}

2. React.FC<Props> (avoid in modern code):

const Button: React.FC<ButtonProps> = ({ label }) => ...

Why avoid React.FC? In older TS versions it automatically added children to every component (even if it shouldn't have any), and it makes the return type ReactElement | null which prevents returning strings/numbers. The explicit approach is more precise.

Typing children correctly:

// Single element
interface WrapperProps {
  children: React.ReactNode   // most permissive — accepts JSX, string, number, null
}

// Render prop / function child
interface ListProps<T> {
  items: T[]
  children: (item: T) => React.ReactNode
}

Event handlers: use React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>, React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement> — these give you the correct event.target type.

Senior tip: use ComponentProps<'button'> or ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> to spread native element props without manually re-typing every HTML attribute.
source: GreatFrontEnd TypeScript + React, Total TypeScript (Matt Pocock), common senior interview

q: What are custom hooks? What rules must they follow and what are the best patterns for building them?
a:
A custom hook is a JavaScript function whose name starts with use that calls other hooks. It's the primary mechanism for extracting and reusing stateful logic between components — without the component hierarchy changes required by render props or HOCs.

Rules: same as built-in hooks — call only at top level, call only from React functions. The use prefix is required for the linter (eslint-plugin-react-hooks) to enforce these rules automatically.

Good patterns:

  • Encapsulate a single concern: useWindowSize, useDebounce, useLocalStorage, useIntersectionObserver
  • Return a stable API tuple or object: return [value, setValue] for state-like hooks; return an object for hooks with multiple outputs
  • Memoize returned callbacks with useCallback so consumers can safely use them as effect dependencies
  • Accept a ref or return a ref for DOM integration: const { ref, isVisible } = useIntersectionObserver(options)
function useDebounce<T>(value: T, delay: number): T {
  const [debouncedValue, setDebouncedValue] = useState(value)
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setTimeout(() => setDebouncedValue(value), delay)
    return () => clearTimeout(id)
  }, [value, delay])
  return debouncedValue
}

Interview framing: custom hooks solve the logic reuse problem. Before hooks, this required HOCs (prop name clashes, wrapper hell) or render props (callback indentation). Hooks compose logic without changing the component tree.
source: React docs (react.dev/learn/reusing-logic-with-custom-hooks), sudheerj Q35, common senior interview

q: Explain the React rendering phases: when does a component render, and when does it commit? What is a 'bailout'?
a:
React rendering has two distinct phases:

Render phase (interruptible): React calls your component function (or render method) to compute the new output. This phase is pure — no side effects, no DOM mutations. React diffs the new virtual tree against the previous one. In Concurrent Mode this phase can be paused, restarted, or abandoned.

Commit phase (synchronous, non-interruptible): React applies the diff to the real DOM. Then it runs useLayoutEffect cleanups and setups, then (after the browser paints) runs useEffect cleanups and setups.

A component re-renders when:

  • Its own state changes (via useState or useReducer)
  • Its parent re-renders (unless it's wrapped in React.memo and props haven't changed)
  • A context it subscribes to changes

Bailout: React skips the render phase for a subtree when it can prove the output would be identical. Mechanisms that trigger bailouts:

  • React.memo — shallow-compares props; if equal, skips rendering the component
  • useState/useReducer — if the new state is the same value (Object.is comparison), React bails out after re-rendering once (it re-renders the component but skips its children and doesn't commit)
  • useMemo — returns the cached value, skipping the computation

Key interview insight: re-rendering is not the same as DOM update. Re-render = calling the function and diffing. DOM update only happens in the commit phase if the diff found actual changes. Many unnecessary re-renders are harmless; optimize only when the profiler shows real cost.
source: React Fiber architecture docs, sudheerj, GreatFrontEnd, common senior interview

q: How would you implement code splitting and lazy loading in a React app? What are the trade-offs?
a:
Code splitting divides your JavaScript bundle into smaller chunks that are loaded on demand, reducing initial load time.

The primary tool is React.lazy + dynamic import():

const Dashboard = React.lazy(() => import('./Dashboard'))

function App() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<PageSkeleton />}>
      <Dashboard />
    </Suspense>
  )
}

Bundlers (Webpack, Vite, Rollup) detect the dynamic import and emit a separate chunk. The chunk is fetched when Dashboard first renders.

Common splitting strategies:

  • Route-level splitting: each route is a separate chunk (most impactful, easiest win)
  • Component-level splitting: heavy components loaded conditionally (rich text editors, charts, code editors)
  • Library splitting: isolate large third-party deps (moment.js, PDF renderers)

Trade-offs:

  • Pro: smaller initial bundle, faster Time to Interactive (TTI)
  • Con: network waterfall on first visit to a route; the chunk must be fetched and parsed before the component renders
  • Mitigation: prefetch chunks on link hover (<link rel="prefetch">) or use router-level prefetching (Next.js does this automatically)

In Next.js App Router: each route segment is automatically split. Use next/dynamic (which wraps React.lazy) for component-level splitting with SSR support. dynamic(() => import('./Chart'), { ssr: false }) loads only on the client.
source: React docs (react.dev/reference/react/lazy), sudheerj Q25, GreatFrontEnd performance section

q: What is prop drilling and what are the patterns to solve it? When is each appropriate?
a:
Prop drilling means passing data through intermediate components that don't use it — just to get it to a deeply nested consumer. The intermediate components become tightly coupled to data they don't own.

Solutions and when to use each:

1. Component composition (best first resort): instead of drilling, pass the already-rendered component as children or as a prop. The top-level component holds the data and renders the leaf; the middle components just slot it in via {children}. No new APIs needed.

// Instead of: <Layout><Sidebar user={user} /></Layout>
<Layout sidebar={<Sidebar user={user} />}>

2. React Context: for data that many components need at different nesting levels and that changes rarely (theme, locale, auth user). Don't use for high-frequency state — every consumer re-renders on any context value change.

3. External state (Zustand, Jotai, Redux): for high-frequency or complex shared state. Components subscribe only to the slices they need (selector pattern), so unrelated components don't re-render.

4. URL state (search params): for UI state that should be shareable/bookmarkable (filters, pagination, selected tab). Lives in the URL, accessible to any component.

Interview framing: reach for composition first — it's the React-idiomatic solution and requires no extra tools. Context for infrequent global state. State manager for complex, frequent, or cross-feature state.
source: React docs (react.dev/learn/passing-data-deeply-with-context), sudheerj, common senior interview

q: How do you test React components effectively? What is the Testing Library philosophy and what should you test?
a:
The core principle of React Testing Library (RTL) is: test the way users interact with your component, not implementation details. Query elements by accessible role, label, text, or test id — not by CSS classes or component internals.

Query priority (RTL docs):

  1. getByRole — reflects the accessibility tree (most preferred)
  2. getByLabelText — form inputs
  3. getByText — non-interactive content
  4. getByTestId — escape hatch for when nothing else works
test('submits the form', async () => {
  render(<LoginForm onSubmit={mockFn} />)
  await userEvent.type(screen.getByLabelText(/email/i), 'a@b.com')
  await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /sign in/i }))
  expect(mockFn).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ email: 'a@b.com' })
})

What to test:

  • User flows (type, click, see result)
  • Conditional rendering (loading state, error state, empty state)
  • Accessibility — roles, aria labels
  • Integration between components

What NOT to test:

  • Internal state values
  • Component method calls
  • Implementation-specific CSS classes

For hooks: use renderHook from RTL. For async operations: use waitFor or findBy* queries (which auto-wait). Mock at the network level with MSW (Mock Service Worker) rather than mocking modules, so tests are closer to real usage.
source: testing-library.com, Kent C. Dodds blog, GreatFrontEnd testing section

q: What are React Server Components (RSC)? How does the client-server component boundary work and what are the data-fetching implications?
a:
React Server Components are components that execute exclusively on the server (during request or build). Their output is a serialized React tree (RSC payload — not HTML) streamed to the client. The client merges this with its existing tree without re-fetching data or re-running the component.

Key properties of Server Components:

  • Zero client-side JavaScript bundle impact — they never ship to the browser
  • Can await data directly (database queries, file system, internal APIs) without useEffect waterfalls
  • Cannot use useState, useEffect, event handlers, or browser APIs
  • Cannot use Context that wraps state

The boundary: 'use client' marks the boundary. Everything in a 'use client' file (and its imports) becomes a Client Component. Critically: a Server Component can import a Client Component, but a Client Component cannot import a Server Component. However, a Client Component can receive a Server Component as children (prop) — the Server Component renders on the server and its output is passed down.

// Server Component — runs on server only
async function ProductPage({ id }: { id: string }) {
  const product = await db.products.findById(id) // direct DB access
  return <ProductCard product={product} />
}

Data fetching implications: fetch in Server Components instead of useEffect to eliminate: (1) client-server roundtrips, (2) loading states for initial data, (3) exposing API secrets to the client. Use Server Actions for mutations. This is the architecture Next.js App Router is built around.
source: React docs (react.dev/learn/server-components), Next.js docs, Josh Comeau RSC article

q: How does useReducer differ from useState, and when should you prefer it? How does it compare to external state managers?
a:
useReducer manages state with a pure reducer function: (state, action) => newState. Suitable when the next state depends on the previous one in complex ways, or when multiple sub-values change together based on the same action.

type Action =
  | { type: 'increment' }
  | { type: 'set'; payload: number }
  | { type: 'reset' }

function reducer(state: number, action: Action): number {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'increment': return state + 1
    case 'set': return action.payload
    case 'reset': return 0
    default: return state
  }
}

const [count, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, 0)

Prefer useReducer over useState when:

  • State is an object with multiple fields that change together
  • The next state depends on the previous state in non-trivial ways
  • You want to decouple event handlers from state update logic (makes testing the reducer trivially easy)
  • You have multiple actions that produce complex state transitions

Prefer useState when:

  • State is a primitive or simple value
  • Updates are independent of each other

vs. Zustand/Redux: useReducer is local to the component tree (or passed via Context). External managers provide a global store that any component can subscribe to without prop threading or Context re-render overhead. Redux DevTools + time travel + middleware (thunks, sagas) add debugging and side-effect capabilities that useReducer alone doesn't have. For shared, cross-feature state — reach for Zustand or Redux.
source: React docs (react.dev/reference/react/useReducer), sudheerj Q28, GreatFrontEnd state section
